title: When the Bagel Calls
text:
The best time to start a tech blog was ten years ago. The second-best time is now.
About three years ago, I was introduced to bioinformatics. My supervisor suggested I research a evolutionary conserved genomic sequence. As the first person in a traditional wet-lab to venture into genomics, I had to learn Linux, R, and how to use bioinformatics databases from scratch—all while conducting experiments. It wasn’t a smooth journey. Even with the wealth of learning resources available online, the problems I encountered weren’t always standard enough to find quick solutions. So, I started documenting my failures and notes in detail, a habit that gradually took root.
Last year, I had the opportunity to study bioinformatics more systematically. With more to learn, I also had more to document. Those notes and lines of code lay quietly in my memos or Notion databases, waiting for me to retrieve them when needed. But I never made them public. At first, I thought the problems that puzzled me were too rookie, too trivial—issues no one else would care about. Later, with the rise of LLMs like ChatGPT and DeepSeek, it seemed even less necessary: you could just type a precise question into a dialog box and get a highly tailored answer within seconds. Did writing a technical blog still matter? Could my content still be helpful to others? The thought, “I’m not skilled enough to produce meaningful content,” lingered like a shadow hovering over me, one I couldn’t shake off.
Then, one day early in 2026, it suddenly hit me: “I think I’m ready.” All the self-doubt vanished. It wasn’t that I woke up feeling overwhelmingly confident, but rather, I felt a natural sense of calling. I knew that organizing, writing, and sharing these insights would make me more complete. And I believe I’m not alone—there must be others, perhaps those standing at the crossroads of wet and dry labs, feeling lost. They might need this.

title: How to Maintain Git and Your Local Code?
text:
Why You Should Manage Versions
When writing code or command-line scripts, I often encounter situations like this:

A script works perfectly 90% of the time, but one line causes problems or could be optimized. After modifying it, the entire script breaks, and I’ve completely forgotten what I changed. The ‘script_90%work’ version is lost, and I have to start over relying on fragmented memory

Sometimes I copy a script to modify it, but without careful naming, my project folder ends up full of scripts like I_did_this_1.0 and I_did_this_2.0. In the end, I have no idea what the differences between them are.
As a wet-lab researcher, I am used to saving many raw images in folders, because by cross-referencing file dates with my lab notebook, I can track what each folder contains. Code is different: if you cannot meticulously log each command and its output, regularly storing different versions of scripts and results is crucial.
In my exploration, I found that Git is a very powerful tool:
By combining Git with GitHub and developing a habit of committing frequently, you essentially create a digital lab notebook. You can easily track historical versions of your scripts, saving a lot of time, effort, and mental overhead.
💡 Version control in Git works in three main steps:

git add <file> — add files to the staging area; these are the files that will be included in the next commit
git commit -m "message" — packages all staged files into a snapshot and saves it in .git
git push origin main — pushes commits from the local branch to the corresponding branch on the remote repository



Learning Resources

Official GitHub help documentation👇
https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/about-github-and-git







An introduction to Git on a Chinese blog👇
https://www.ruanyifeng.com/blog/2018/10/git-internals.html



Basic Workflow for Pushing Local Code to GitHub

Log in to GitHub and create a repository. Adding a README or .gitignore is optional (you can also create them locally and push later).
Initialize Git in your local project folder. If you are using linux system:

# 0. Create local project directory
mkdir Sequence_Processing_Tool_Project
cd Sequence_Processing_Tool_Project

Use Git to manage files and push them to the remote repository.




Source: Lulu Ilmaknun Qurotaini, “Meme Git Compilation”




Common Git Commands
# 1. Initialize a Git repository
git init  # Make sure you are in the correct project folder
# If you are in the wrong folder, remove the repository
rm -rf .git

# 2. Add files to the staging area
git add .  # Track the entire folder, or specific files: git add <file_name>

# 3. Commit changes locally
git commit -m "Initial commit: add sequence processing tool and scripts"

# 4. Link to a remote repository
git remote add origin https://github.com/yaqi-jiao/SeqProcessingTool.git
git remote -v  # Verify the remote repository

# Expected output
# origin  git@github.com:yaqi-jiao/Sequence_Processing_Tool_Project.git (fetch)
# origin  git@github.com:yaqi-jiao/Sequence_Processing_Tool_Project.git (push)

# 5. Set main branch and push
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

# 6. Check status and manage staging
git status  # View staged files
git reset   # Unstage all files
git restore --staged data/ result/  # Remove unwanted files from staging
git restore --staged data/sample.txt


Branch Management
By default, GitHub uses the main branch.
# Create a new branch
git checkout -b feature_x

# Make changes in this branch, then push with:
git push -u origin feature_x


Cloning a Repository from GitHub
If your local repository and GitHub are out of sync, first pull the remote repository, merge changes, then push. Conflicts may occur if local and remote files differ. Files with conflicts will appear highlighted; edit them manually, then add and commit before pushing.
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories


Tips for Using Git Effectively

Start with a well-organized local project folder.
Avoid deleting files directly on GitHub. Delete locally and sync with Git.
Write a README file for each repository.
To back up R scripts, create an RProject and select create a git repository. You can then commit files from RStudio, but pushing still requires the terminal.
Git works equally well on Linux and servers for code management.

title: About Bagel
text:
In Everything Everywhere All at Once, the protagonist’s daughter Joy—who also serves as the film’s ultimate antagonist—uses her powers to compress the entire universe onto a single bagel, creating an all-consuming void. Through it, she confronts the truth of life: “nothing matters.” That’s the infinite potential of the bagel.
Leaving aside the film’s deeper themes of chaos, existential crisis, and nihilism, I was left with one irresistible urge: I also want to make a bagel, a place where I gather everything from my journey through bioinformatics.

What can you find through this bagel?
TIL (Today I Learned): Curated notes and useful bits I pick up along the way in bioinformatics.
TIF (Things I Have Found): Notes on insightful papers—ideas worth remembering and building upon.
TIB (Things I Have Built): Projects I’m working on, from early sketches to functional tools.
Milestone: Personal victories, progress updates, and moments worth celebrating.
Misc: Non-technical musings, occasional reflections, and whatever else fits the mood.
…and perhaps more to come.
After all, you can put everything on a bagel!!

title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
This article contains my study notes for the free online course “Essence of Linear Algebra” by the YouTube channel 3Blue1Brown. I consider it to be one of the best introductory resources on the subject. Prior to this, my understanding of matrices and equations was largely confined to rote formula manipulation. This video series fundamentally changed my perspective, inspiring me to view linear algebra through the lens of geometric transformations. Not only is this more intuitive, but it often makes problem-solving simpler! As a researcher in biology, this makes perfect sense to me—humans are more sensitive to and understand concrete, visualizable concepts (animation > graphics > numbers > abstract symbols) more quickly and deeply.
To honor the spirit of this tutorial and highlight the geometric nature of linear algebra, I will strive to explain concepts from both algebraic and geometric viewpoints wherever possible.
Due to the volume of content, these notes will be published in two parts.

objectID: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#what-is-a-vector
href: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#what-is-a-vector
title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
1. What is a Vector?

Geometric Perspective: An arrow in space with a specific length (magnitude) and direction. A vector’s essence is unchanged by translation.
Algebraic/Coordinate Perspective: An ordered list of numbers (e.g., \([x, y]\)) that describes how to reach the tip of the arrow from its tail by scaling and adding the basis vectors of a chosen coordinate system. This defines operations like vector addition and scalar multiplication.
Computer Science Perspective: Simply an ordered list of numbers, a data structure.

💡 Key insight: The numerical representation of a vector implicitly depends on our choice of basis vectors.

title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
2. Linear Combination, Span, and Basis
In the standard Cartesian coordinate system, we implicitly use the basis vectors \(\hat{i} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\hat{j} = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\). By scaling and adding \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\), we can construct any vector in the plane.

Linear Combination: The result of scaling and adding vectors. For example, \(a\vec{v} + b\vec{w}\) is a linear combination of \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{w}\).
Span: The set of all possible linear combinations of a given set of vectors. It answers the question: “What are all the vectors you can reach using only vector addition and scalar multiplication?”






Geometric Outcomes for the Span of Two Vectors:

Two non-zero, non-collinear vectors: Their span is the entire 2D plane.
Two non-zero, collinear vectors: Their span is the line they lie on.
Two zero vectors: Their span is just the origin.

Linear (In)dependence:

Geometric Perspective: A set of vectors is linearly dependent if at least one vector “lies in the span” of the others, adding no new directional information. Otherwise, they are linearly independent.
Algebraic Perspective: A set of vectors \(\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, ..., \vec{v}_n\}\) is linearly dependent if there exists a set of scalars \(\{c_1, c_2, ..., c_n\}\), NOT all zero, such that \(c_1\vec{v}_1 + c_2\vec{v}_2 + ... + c_n\vec{v}_n = \vec{0}\). This is equivalent to saying one vector can be written as a linear combination of the others.

title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
3. Matrices as Linear Transformations
💡 Note: “Transformation” is an intuitive synonym for “function,” suggesting we can understand input-output relationships through the movement and deformation of space.
A Linear Transformation is a mapping that satisfies two key properties:

Lines remain lines: All straight lines (including diagonals) remain straight after the transformation; they do not curve.
Origin remains fixed: The origin point \((0,0)\) stays at \((0,0)\).
(Geometrically, these are equivalent to: Grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced.)

How to Describe Linear Transformations Numerically:
The critical insight: Since any vector can be expressed as a linear combination of basis vectors, if you know where the basis vectors \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\) land after the transformation, you can deduce where any vector lands.
Understanding Matrices:

Geometric Perspective: A matrix represents a specific linear transformation rule.
Algebraic Perspective: A matrix is an array of numbers that encodes, in coordinate form, where the basis vectors go. The columns of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix are precisely the coordinates of the transformed \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\).

title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
4. Matrix Multiplication as Composition
Applying two linear transformations in succession (e.g., rotation \(\mathbf{A}\), then shear \(\mathbf{B}\)) results in a new, composite linear transformation. The matrix for this new transformation is the product of the original matrices.

Geometric Perspective: Matrix multiplication corresponds to composition of linear transformations (doing one transformation, then another).
Algebraic Perspective: The computational rule \(\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\vec{v}) = (\mathbf{BA})\vec{v}\) is the numerical realization of this composition, following the same order as function composition \(f(g(x))\).
💡 Note: Matrix multiplication is read from right to left.




To compute the product matrix \(\mathbf{M}_2\mathbf{M}_1\): 1. The first column is obtained by applying \(\mathbf{M}_2\) to the first column of \(\mathbf{M}_1\) (where \(\hat{i}\) lands after \(\mathbf{M}_1\)); 2. The second column is obtained by applying \(\mathbf{M}_2\) to the second column of \(\mathbf{M}_1\) (where \(\hat{j}\) lands after \(\mathbf{M}_1\))

objectID: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#determinant
href: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#determinant
title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
5. Determinant
A linear transformation stretches or squishes space. The determinant measures this scaling factor.

Geometric Perspective: The absolute value of the determinant represents the factor by which areas (in 2D) or volumes (in 3D) are scaled. The sign indicates whether the orientation of space is flipped (like turning a paper over).
💡 Attention: The determinant is defined only for \(n \times n\) (square) matrices! The concept of a “volume/area scaling factor” intrinsically requires a transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to itself.
Algebraic Perspective: For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}a & b\\c & d\end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is calculated as \(ad - bc\), whose geometric meaning is the area scaling/orientation described above.






Interpreting the Determinant’s Value:

\(\det(\mathbf{A}) > 1\): Area expands, orientation preserved.
\(\det(\mathbf{A}) = 1\): Area unchanged, orientation preserved (e.g., pure rotation).
\(0 < \det(\mathbf{A}) < 1\): Area contracts, orientation preserved.
\(\det(\mathbf{A}) = 0\): Space is compressed onto a lower dimension. The transformation is non-invertible.
\(\det(\mathbf{A}) < 0\): Area is scaled, and orientation is flipped. The absolute value gives the scaling factor.

objectID: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#inverse-matrices
href: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#inverse-matrices
title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
6. Inverse Matrices





Consider the linear system \(\mathbf{A}\vec{x} = \vec{v}\).






Geometric Perspective: Given a transformation \(\mathbf{A}\) and an output \(\vec{v}\), finding the input \(\vec{x}\) that was transformed into \(\vec{v}\) is equivalent to finding the inverse transformation \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\), which maps \(\vec{v}\) back to \(\vec{x}\).
Algebraic Perspective: This inverse transformation corresponds to the inverse matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\). Solving for \(\vec{x}\) becomes the computation \(\vec{x} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\vec{v}\).

Identity Transformation and Invertibility:

The Identity Transformation does nothing, leaving all vectors unchanged. Its matrix is \(\mathbf{I}\).
If the inverse of \(\mathbf{A}\) exists, then applying \(\mathbf{A}\) followed by \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) (or vice versa) results in the identity transformation: \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}\).
💡 Key Condition: An inverse matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) exists if and only if \(\det(\mathbf{A}) \neq 0\). If \(\det(\mathbf{A}) = 0\), the transformation collapses space, information is lost, and there is no unique way to reverse the process.

objectID: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#rank-and-column-space
href: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#rank-and-column-space
title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
7. Rank and Column Space

Column Space: The span of all column vectors of a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\). Geometrically, it is the set of all possible output vectors \(\mathbf{A}\vec{x}\). It answers: “After transformation \(\mathbf{A}\), where can all vectors land?”
Rank: The dimension of the column space. It describes the dimensionality of the output space after the transformation.

Example: If the output of a transformation is a line, its rank is 1. If the output is a plane, its rank is 2.
The rank of an \(m \times n\) matrix cannot exceed \(\min(m, n)\).


A matrix is Full Rank if its rank equals its number of columns (\(n\)). This means the transformation does not collapse any dimension within the input space.
For an \(n \times n\) Square Matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the following are equivalent:

Determinant Condition: \(\det(\mathbf{A}) \neq 0\)
Rank Condition: \(\mathbf{A}\) is full rank, i.e., \(\text{rank}(\mathbf{A}) = n\)
Invertibility Condition: \(\mathbf{A}\) is invertible (i.e., \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) exists)

objectID: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#null-space
href: posts/Course notes_Essence of Linear Algebra Pt1/index.html#null-space
title: Course note: Essence of Linear Algebra, Pt.1
text:
8. Null Space

Null Space: The set of all input vectors that get mapped to the zero vector under transformation \(\mathbf{A}\): \(\{\vec{x} \mid \mathbf{A}\vec{x} = \vec{0}\}\).
Geometric Meaning: These are the vectors that are “compressed flat” or “annihilated” by the transformation. If the null space contains more than just the zero vector, the transformation is many-to-one, which is the essence of its non-invertibility when \(\det(\mathbf{A})=0\).







💡 Summary of Core Ideas:

A 【Linear Transformation】 is a way to manipulate space that keeps grid lines parallel and evenly spaced and fixes the origin.
A 【Matrix】 is the numerical language for describing such a transformation; its columns represent the coordinates of the transformed basis vectors.

Every system of linear equations \(\mathbf{A}\vec{x} = \vec{v}\) is associated with a linear transformation \(\mathbf{A}\).

When \(\det(\mathbf{A}) \neq 0\) (transformation is invertible), a unique inverse \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) exists to solve the system.
When \(\det(\mathbf{A}) = 0\) (transformation collapses dimensions):

The Column Space tells us what kind of \(\vec{v}\) could have a solution (\(\vec{v}\) must be in the column space).
The Null Space describes the structure of all possible solutions if they exist: any particular solution plus any vector from the null space.

title: How to present statistical analysis results properly?
text:
After a nerve-wracking month of waiting, my grade for BIOS15 (Processing and Analysis of Biological Data) is finally out! I received a VG🎉, which was not easy, especially since my initial grades for the scientific report writing assignments were quite low. After spending a huge amount of time catching up on statistics and R programming—finally understanding what Linear Regression and (Generalized) linear mixed models actually do—and successfully turning the results into decent-looking graphs with ggplot2 and LaTeX, I still needed to describe them in a scientific, intuitive, and easy-to-understand way. And this is the most important part of making your analysis accessible to both peers and the general public.
After taking this course, I realized that I had received very little training like this in my previous regenerative biology lab. Even when senior PhD students in the research group presented their results and mentioned statistical data, the information I got was often something like, “Compared to the single mutant, the myocardial cells in double mutant zebrafish regenerated significantly 60 days after cardiac surgery,” rather than the more appropriate “The myocardial cells in double mutant zebrafish regenerated by xx% 60 days after cardiac surgery.” This might be another major difference between wet-lab and dry-lab analysis: histology staining results on a PPT seem self-evident, so I never actively considered whether these images and findings needed statistical support. I think that if one wants to transition from wet-lab to dry-lab work, it’s essential to learn how to present analysis results smartly; otherwise, your conclusions may lack credibility.
Here are some takeaways I had after the course👇:

R Markdown and LaTeX are truly amazing! R Markdown saves a lot of time on formatting
Research hypotheses and well-defined research questions are crucial! Of course, when you’re staring at a bunch of numbers, it’s hard to come up with meaningful hypotheses. That’s why early data exploration (summary statistics and graphical exploration) is essential to understand their patterns and distributions.
Before fitting specific models, spend some time understanding your variables. Are they continuous or discrete? This influences model selection! Pay attention to the units of the variables and what they actually represent, as this affects the choice of predictors and responses.




Make a variable table can also help your reader. Source: my final report



In the introduction, clearly state the research background and objectives.
In the methods section, specify the purpose of each method and explain how they were applied. And this will also help you better understand what you are doing.
In the results section: quantify the effects for variables relevant to the research question! Effect size is expressed through standard deviation, so if you want to describe the impact of a specific variable on the response, you can calculate the predicted value for the mean of the response and some contrast, like +1 SD.




That’s how I quantify the effects in my final report



For all statistically significant results, provide a biological interpretation. Explain what these numbers mean biologically, since you are, after all, a biology researcher!
Avoid ambiguous abbreviations in tables and figures; write out the variable names. Captions are often overlooked but are essential—explain everything in the table/figure clearly.
After writing, check for duplicate abbreviations and shorthand. For example, don’t use “GLMM” in one part of the report and “(Generalized) linear mixed model” in another. Write out the full term the first time it appears, followed by the abbreviation in parentheses, and then use the abbreviation consistently thereafter.
Comment your code clearly!
Image size matters. Sometimes you need to make trade-offs to ensure the main report is easy to read. Additional material can be included as supplementary.




Bad example! When I want to put too much information in my figure. Here’s teacher’s comment: “Nice but complex figure. I think it would look nicer if it was about half the height, so that the biplots are square and the loading plots could be more compact too”



Don’t spend too much time learning ggplot2 from the bottom up. It’s a package better mastered through practice.
